blocks.text: Imagine a bustling city with roads connecting various neighborhoods. Each vehicle knows its destination, but how do they find the best route? In computer networks, switches play a similar role, directing data frames to their correct destinations efficiently.

blocks.markdown: In this lesson, we will explore how switches operate within a network, focusing on how they learn and use MAC addresses to forward frames. We will also compare switches with hubs and routers, and delve into the structure of an Ethernet frame.

blocks.title: MAC Address
blocks.text: A Media Access Control (MAC) address is a unique identifier assigned to network interfaces for communications on the physical network segment. It is typically represented as a 48-bit hexadecimal number.

blocks.markdown: Switches are network devices that forward data frames based on MAC addresses. Unlike hubs, which broadcast frames to all ports, switches intelligently direct frames to the appropriate port, reducing network congestion and improving efficiency.

blocks.title: Switch Learning Process
blocks.text: Switches learn which MAC addresses are reachable through which ports by examining the source MAC address of incoming frames and updating their MAC address table accordingly.

blocks.title: Switch Learning Example
blocks.prompt: Consider a switch with three ports: Port 1, Port 2, and Port 3. A frame with source MAC address A arrives at Port 1. How does the switch update its MAC address table?

steps.text: Initially, the switch's MAC address table is empty.
The switch receives a frame with source MAC address A on Port 1.
The switch updates its MAC address table to associate MAC address A with Port 1.

blocks.answer: The switch's MAC address table now contains an entry associating MAC address A with Port 1.

blocks.markdown: Switches differ from routers in that they operate at the data link layer (Layer 2) of the OSI model, while routers operate at the network layer (Layer 3). This distinction allows switches to forward frames based on MAC addresses, whereas routers use IP addresses.

rows: Forwards frames to specific ports based on MAC addresses
Routes packets based on IP addresses

blocks.markdown: An Ethernet frame is the basic unit of data transmission in Ethernet networks. It consists of several fields, including the destination and source MAC addresses, EtherType, payload, and Frame Check Sequence (FCS).

blocks.title: Ethernet Frame Structure
blocks.text: An Ethernet frame typically includes the following fields: Preamble, Destination MAC Address, Source MAC Address, EtherType, Payload, and Frame Check Sequence (FCS).

blocks.title: Ethernet Frame Analysis
blocks.prompt: Given an Ethernet frame with the following fields: Destination MAC: 00:14:22:01:23:45, Source MAC: 00:16:36:11:22:33, EtherType: 0x0800, Payload: 'Hello', FCS: 0x1A2B3C4D. Identify the purpose of each field.

steps.text: The Destination MAC Address (00:14:22:01:23:45) specifies the intended recipient of the frame.
The Source MAC Address (00:16:36:11:22:33) indicates the sender of the frame.
The EtherType (0x0800) specifies the protocol of the payload, in this case, IPv4.
The Payload ('Hello') contains the actual data being transmitted.
The Frame Check Sequence (FCS: 0x1A2B3C4D) is used for error checking.

blocks.answer: Each field in the Ethernet frame serves a specific purpose: Destination MAC for recipient, Source MAC for sender, EtherType for protocol identification, Payload for data, and FCS for error checking.

blocks.title: Broadcast Storms
blocks.text: In networks with multiple switches, improper configuration can lead to broadcast storms, where frames are continuously circulated, overwhelming the network.

points: Switches learn MAC addresses by examining incoming frames and updating their MAC address tables.
Switches operate at Layer 2, forwarding frames based on MAC addresses, unlike routers that operate at Layer 3 using IP addresses.
An Ethernet frame includes fields such as destination and source MAC addresses, EtherType, payload, and FCS.
